Empirical Research Plan:  Housing‐wealth shocks and college enrollment  
(PSID households, late-1990s–early-2000s)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy:  Two-stage least squares (2SLS) panel IV exploiting geographic
variation in house-price movements.

• First stage:  Regress household i’s liquid housing wealth (home equity or
housing wealth / income) on the interaction of (i) the MSA-level repeat-sales
house-price index (HPI) growth and (ii) the household’s lagged house value.
   –  Intuition:  Within an MSA-year, every homeowner experiences the same %
     price shock, but the dollar shock differs by the size of the house owned
     ex-ante.  
   –  Because renters have zero baseline value, the instrument generates no
     predicted wealth change for them, letting renters serve as an internal
     control group inside the first stage.

• Second stage:  Use the predicted (instrumented) change in housing wealth to
explain the binary indicator that the household’s college-age child enrolls in
college in t + 1.

Why IV rather than plain DiD?
1. Avoids endogeneity of actual refinancing/borrowing decisions that translate
   price gains into liquid wealth.  
2. Spatial price growth is largely driven by supply-side constraints,
   demographics, and national interest-rate shocks—factors plausibly unrelated
   to a given family’s propensity to send a child to college.

Robustness:  Augment with a homeowner × (post-boom) difference-in-differences
and an event-study graph to show pre-trend balance.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable:  ∆LiquidHousingWealth_it  = change in real housing equity
(= current market value – outstanding mortgage principal) divided by pre-period
income.

Instrument (Z_it):  Predicted dollar change  
                      = HPI_growth_mst × lagged_house_value_it–1  
                      (0 for renters).

Control group (counterfactual): Renters in the same MSA-year (their Z_it = 0)
plus homeowners in low-appreciation MSAs serve as additional variation.

Treatment timing:  Annual; use t – 1 to t changes so that shocks precede the
fall semester enrollment decision in year t.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument relevance:  Local HPI growth strongly predicts changes in owner
home equity.  Highly plausible and testable (first-stage F ≫ 10 is expected).

A2. Exclusion (exogeneity):  Conditional on fixed effects and controls, MSA-year
house-price growth affects a household’s college-enrollment decision only
through its impact on liquid housing wealth—not through other local shocks that
also shift enrollment.  Plausible because:
   • Labor-market shocks are controlled by MSA-year unemployment rates.  
   • Cohort fixed effects absorb national trends in college attendance.

A3. Independence (no omitted variables correlated with Z_it):  Including
household FE eliminates time-invariant unobservables like parental valuation of
education; MSA-year FE absorb common local shocks.

A4. Monotonicity:  A positive HPI shock cannot reduce housing wealth for any
homeowner.  Holds mechanically.

A5. SUTVA:  One family’s housing-wealth shock does not directly change another
family’s college decision except through general-equilibrium paths already
captured by MSA-year FE.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Local labor-market or tuition shocks correlated with house prices  
   Mitigation:  Add MSA-year controls—unemployment, median wage, public tuition
   levels; include MSA-year fixed effects in some specs.

T2. Anticipation / timing mismatch (families time college relative to expected
     future price gains)  
   Mitigation:  Use one-year leads and lags of the instrument in an event-study
   specification to test for pre-trends; restrict sample to families with no
   kids already in college at baseline.

T3. Sample selection (only families that remain in the PSID or do not move
     between MSAs)  
   Mitigation:  Use household fixed effects and include movers with the HPI of
   their origin MSA; show robustness to dropping movers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast data handling
library(fixest)         # high-speed FE & IV estimation
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load PSID panel --------------------------------------------------------
psid <- fread("psid_housing_edu.csv")   # one row per household-year

# 2. Variable construction --------------------------------------------------
psid[, year          := as.integer(year)]
psid[, id            := as.integer(fam_id)]
psid[, age_child18_22:= (child_age >= 18 & child_age <= 22)]   # sample filter

# Housing equity and instrument
psid[, equity        := pmax(0, house_value - mortgage_bal)]
psid[, equity_lag    := shift(equity, 1, type = "lag"), by = id]
psid[, hpi_growth    := (msa_hpi / shift(msa_hpi,1)) - 1, by = msa]

psid[, d_equity      := (equity - equity_lag) / income_lag]
psid[, Z             := hpi_growth * equity_lag / income_lag]  # 0 for renters

# Outcome
psid[, enroll        := as.integer(child_enrolled == 1)]

# Sample restrictions -------------------------------------------------------
sample <- psid[age_child18_22 == TRUE & !is.na(d_equity) & !is.na(enroll)]

# 3. Main 2SLS specification -----------------------------------------------
iv_main <- feols(enroll ~ 1 | d_equity ~ Z,
                 data = sample,
                 cluster = ~msa)

summary(iv_main)

# 4. Robustness:  add MSA-year FE ------------------------------------------
iv_fe <- feols(enroll ~ 1 | d_equity ~ Z | id + msa^year,
               data = sample,
               cluster = ~msa)

summary(iv_fe)

# 5. Robustness:  placebo pre-trend test ------------------------------------
# lead of Z (should be 0 effect)
sample[, Z_lead := shift(Z, -1), by = id]

iv_placebo <- feols(enroll ~ 1 | d_equity ~ Z_lead,
                    data = sample,
                    cluster = ~msa)

summary(iv_placebo)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (liquidity constraints) predicts a positive effect: a $10,000
increase in liquid housing wealth should raise enrollment probability.  Prior
literature (e.g., Lovenheim 2011) finds elasticities around 2–4 percentage
points per $100k (≈0.02–0.04).  For our normalized variable (∆equity / income),
I expect a semi-elasticity of roughly 0.05; i.e., a one-standard-deviation
increase in equity (~0.5 × income) raises enrollment by ≈2.5 pp.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Relevance (first-stage F > 10) ………………………………………… 1  
C2. Exogeneity / independence of Z ……………………………………… 0.7  
C3. Exclusion restriction (no other channels) ………………………… 0.6  
C4. Monotonicity (no “defiers”) ………………………………………… 1  
C5. SUTVA (no spillovers) ………………………………………………… 0.8  

Overall, while relevance and monotonicity are strong, the chief concerns are
possible local labor-market channels and household migration, which motivate the
robustness checks outlined above.
